verses.text: As God's fellow workers, then, we urge you not to receive God's grace in vain.
For He says: "In the time of favor I heard you, and in the day of salvation I helped you." Behold, now is the time of favor; now is the day of salvation!
We put no obstacle in anyone's way, so that no one can discredit our ministry.
Rather, as servants of God we commend ourselves in every way: in great endurance; in troubles, hardships, and calamities;
in beatings, imprisonments, and riots; in labor, sleepless nights, and hunger;
in purity, knowledge, patience, and kindness; in the Holy Spirit and in sincere love;
in truthful speech and in the power of God; with the weapons of righteousness in the right hand and in the left;
through glory and dishonor, slander and praise; viewed as imposters, yet genuine;
as unknown, yet well-known; dying, and yet we live on; punished, yet not killed;
sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; poor, yet making many rich; having nothing, and yet possessing everything.
We have spoken freely to you, Corinthians. Our hearts are open wide.
It is not our affection, but yours, that is restrained.
As a fair exchange, I ask you as my children: Open wide your hearts also.
Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership can righteousness have with wickedness? Or what fellowship does light have with darkness?
What harmony is there between Christ and Belial? Or what does a believer have in common with an unbeliever?

What agreement can exist between the temple of God and idols? For we are the temple of the living God. As God has said: "I will dwell with them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they will be My people."
"Therefore come out from among them and be separate, says the Lord. Touch no unclean thing, and I will receive you."
And: "I will be a Father to you, and you will be My sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty."

context.author: Paul the apostle, with Timothy (1:1)
context.genre: Letter, personal and defensive, among Paul’s most emotional
context.audience: The church in Corinth, after a painful period of conflict
context.setting: Paul appeals for the Corinthians to respond to God’s grace, listing his own hardships as an example of faithful service. He asks them to open their hearts as he has opened his, and warns them not to be “unequally yoked” with unbelievers, a phrase about partnership in pagan worship.
context.custom: Many scholars hear an echo of Deuteronomy 22:10, which forbids yoking an ox with a donkey, in Paul’s warning against partnerships that mix pagan worship with the worship of Christ. First Corinthians 8 and 10 show that some Corinthian Christians were invited to temple dinners, and some felt free to go.
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 7 returns to Paul’s heart and his joy at the good news Titus brought.
context.timelineBible: Verse 2 quotes Isaiah 49:8, “in the day of salvation I helped you.” Verses 16-18 collect Old Testament promises (Leviticus 26:11-12; Isaiah 52:11; 2 Samuel 7:14).
context.sparkNotes: Paul urges the Corinthians not to receive God’s grace in vain, because now is the day of salvation. He lists the hardships he has endured as servant of God. His heart is open to them, and he asks for theirs in return. He warns them not to be yoked together with unbelievers, because God’s temple has nothing to do with idols.

translation.meaning: Mismatched under one yoke, from a word meaning a different kind of harness partner.
A name for Satan, from a Hebrew word meaning worthlessness.

otBackground.note: “In the day of salvation I helped you.”
Do not plow with an ox and a donkey together.

overview.summary: Now is the day of salvation. Paul commends his ministry through hardship, asks the Corinthians to open their hearts, and warns them against partnership with idolatry.
overview.settingLine: Paul writes from Macedonia to the church in Corinth.

history.t: The nine hardships in vv.4-5 are among several such lists Paul gave (11:23-29; Romans 8:35).
Pagan temples hosted banquets that business associates attended.

customs.t: Two animals pulled a plow together, so mismatched pairs made the work harder.
The hearts and affections were thought to be in the chest and “cramped” or “wide.”

archaeology.t: Wooden yokes and plowing scenes appear on Greek pottery.
A healing temple with banquet rooms.

overview.discussion: Paul says, “We have opened wide our hearts to you.” Is there a relationship where I’ve kept my heart shut and might take the first step?
overview.book: The second letter to the Corinthians · 13 chapters. Paul’s most personal letter, written to heal a strained relationship.
overview.author: Paul

historicalImage.caption: Ploughing in the Nivernais, by Rosa Bonheur (1849), with teams of yoked oxen. Paul writes "Do not be yoked together with unbelievers" (2 Corinthians 6:14). Many scholars hear an echo of Deuteronomy 22:10, which forbids ploughing with an ox and a donkey together.
